speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: My answer will also address written Question No 36 from today's Order paper, oral Question Nos 20 and 21 and written Question No 53 raised by Mr Louis Ng from the Order Paper on 1 August.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I believe it is also not too late to wish all nurses in Singapore, Happy Nurses' Day.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Over the last five years, there has been a slight overall increase in the attrition rates for local nurses.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The typical nurse-to-bed ratio for general wards in the public acute hospitals is one nurse for every four or five beds.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The typical nurse-to-patient ratio in the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) in the public acute hospitals is one nurse for each ICU patient and could be higher, such as two nurses for more complex ICU cases.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This has not changed significantly over the past five years.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Ng has asked for salary comparison between private and public hospital nurses.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We are reluctant to provide this so openly, as we know that both sectors compete for manpower.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We also do not have data for the private sector.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I will, however, share a few data points.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Staff Nurses (SNs) and Senior Staff Nurses (SSNs) form the largest proportion of our nursing workforce.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In general, it takes an average four to six years for a fresh graduate to move up to SSN.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Hence, an SN in 2017 may be drawing the annual salary in the SSN range by 2021.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The key issue is to retain the services of nurses.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Our strategy to stabilise the nursing workforce covers several key aspects.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: These include reviewing the scope of work that nurses are doing to enable them to spend more time on direct patient care.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Equally important is to ensure that remunerations are competitive, locally and also internationally.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: On reviewing the scope of work, our public healthcare institutions adopt a multi-prong approach to reduce the administrative workload for nurses and enable nurses to focus on patient care.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This includes streamlining care processes and deploying dedicated administrative and support care staff to assist nurses.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Over time, we have also introduced innovations in automation, technology, robotics and AI-enabled technology to assist nurses and healthcare staff, to ease the load of non-clinical and administrative tasks.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: An example of such technology is the Nursing Software Suite, introduced by Singapore Health Services (SHS) in their hospitals to enable patients to self-help, such as enabling them to check their results, medications, schedules for tests and indicating their requests to the care team.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Other than reviewing the job scope and administrative workload, as our population ages, there will continue to be growing demands on healthcare manpower.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I also urge families and caregivers to be a partner in the care journey of your loved ones, as working together with us will help alleviate the workload faced by our healthcare staff.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked if the National Wellness Committee for Junior Doctors (NWC-JD) could broaden its scope of work to include the working hours and conditions of nurses.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We would like to explain that the NWC-JD was formed to specifically address issues related to junior doctors.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: These need to be tackled differently in the case of junior doctors because of their regular rotations across the public healthcare system, compared to other staff groups who are employed directly by the respective public healthcare clusters.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: MOH and the public healthcare clusters have always been concerned about the well-being of nurses and other staff groups.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For example, we had formed an internal cross-cluster Staff Well-being Committee in 2019 for clusters to share best practices with one another and provide feedback to MOH on enhancements to improve well-being across all categories of staff.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: One example of its recommendations was for MOH to look deeper into the issues of abuse and harassment of healthcare workers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Hence, we announced earlier in March 2022 the formation of a Tripartite Workgroup to address this nationally.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Clusters have also enhanced their support measures for staff.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For example, Chief Wellness Officers have been appointed by clusters to oversee and develop system changes to improve the well-being of all healthcare staff.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Counselling services, peer-support networks and staff support assistance plans have also been put in place to support staff.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The rest day provisions and work hour limits for public healthcare workers are stipulated in the Employment Act or set out in the public healthcare clusters' employment contracts, as previously explained to Mr Louis Ng in Parliament, in March.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: While the Ministry does not impose a minimum number of rest hours, duty rosters for nurses are planned in advance to ensure staff have adequate rest between shifts.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Even as we prioritise the well-being of our nurses, we appreciate the reality of their work, which is to deliver timely and quality patient care.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Ministry is working to ensure there are sufficient nurses on the ground.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We understand the importance of recognising nurses' contributions and the Ministry has worked on reviewing their salaries and allowances.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: With the easing of COVID-19, public healthcare institutions have been allowing nurses to take time off work to rest and recover.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This includes allowing foreign staff to return home to spend time with their loved ones, after a long period of time away from them in 2020 and 2021, when many borders were closed and travel restrictions were in effect.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We know from clusters' data that leave is being approved and allowed.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: MOH remains committed to provide support to the public healthcare clusters in our efforts to ensure that there is sufficient manpower on the ground, and look after the well-being of our nurses, as they continue to face pressures from COVID-19 surge waves and an ageing population.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One, the Senior Parliamentary Secretary mentioned that the nurses should have adequate rest.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But I am just wondering whether MOH can clarify what "adequate" means.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I think a lot of nurses are sharing that they sometimes end their shift at 9.00 pm or 10.00 pm, and then they are back at work at 7.00 am, and that is insufficient rest for many of them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Two, can I ask whether MOH has an ideal nurse-to-patient ratio and what are we doing to work towards that ideal ratio, both in the general wards and the ICUs as well?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, for the ancillary care staff, I asked for their median salary as well, but I understand we cannot provide.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Still, I think they do help in reducing the nurses' workload.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, if I could ask the Senior Parliamentary Secretary what is MOH doing in terms of increasing the salary of the ancillary care staff, their career progression, as well as increasing the hiring of these staff members.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There are many different arrangements within the public healthcare institutions in the different clusters on how they actually manage the rest hours amongst the healthcare workers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, in some clusters, it is about ensuring that they typically work on rotating shifts and they are rostered such that they have adequate rest time within shifts.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Guidance has also been given, so that they are given rest time for their breaks.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Duty rosters are planned in advance and there are guidelines, so that they are not working consecutively beyond a certain number of days so that they get the rest they needed.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Within the working space, they are also given dedicated hall rooms, staggered break times so that they can have sufficient rest.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The reality on the ground is that there are many challenges and these nurses work very hard.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There are realities of their workplaces that require them to go beyond their call of duty.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We really appreciate that and we know that it has been challenging for the nurses and all the healthcare workers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, the key thing is making sure that there is a sufficient number on the ground and that is something that we are continually looking at.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The attrition rate is a reflection of this.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The second question is related to the ideal nurse-to-patient ratio.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This is a function of the type of wards and the work that they do, because it is a function of the care that is needed for the patient.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: And, as you know, they are all tiered in terms of what specific care needs to be given.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, this is a function of those two.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: And that is a priority because patient care is important.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, in a lot of the settings, what we are trying to do is also ensuring that they have sufficient time to dedicate to patient care.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: What are the other pieces of work that they need to do?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: For administrative work, we are looking at various ways on how we can manage some of this work, so that there is sufficient time and they are able to dedicate their time to the work in relation to patient care.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In relation to the Member's concern and queries with regard to salaries, and also that of the other workers, the healthcare workers, I think this is something that we are constantly looking at because we know how valuable they are in our community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We are concerned about the pandemic still being around and also the fact that we have an ageing population.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, this is something we are constantly looking at, at making this sector a favourable one, something that is attractive, so that we can have people go into the sector and relieve the manpower on the ground.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: But the reality is, as I have mentioned earlier, we are doing everything.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The issue that we are seeing right now is the fact that we are losing foreign nurses due to the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Now that the borders are open, they can go back.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: They are also being attracted by prospects overseas.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, there is international competition and we are losing all these workers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: MOH remains committed to trying to look at this issue holistically and adopt a multi-pronged approach in improving the situation on the ground.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I do agree that we have a lot of guidelines in place.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: But I think it is very difficult to follow at this point because, as the Senior Parliamentary Secretary mentioned, a lot of the foreign nurses are leaving and that really puts the stress now on the local nurses.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: So, we can rely on their passion, they are very passionate about it, but I think they are really urging for some protection, especially of their rest time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Again, I ask whether MOH can, at least, make sure that the guidelines on adequate rest for nurses are being adhered to at this point.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: And amongst some of the issues raised is clearly the issue of giving sufficient rest to the nurses.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: And this is something that they are looking at.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The implementation of these different recommendations is being rolled out and we do hope to see that these recommendations and proposals are impacting the workflow and, hopefully, they will improve outcomes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: On the other hand, there are also other things that we hope to see, because I also mentioned earlier about how family members, there is a certain expectation of what nurses are expected to do in hospitals and this also does not help in terms of adding to their workload.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Hopefully, through all these efforts that we are putting up, there is improvement and we will constantly review this to see how it has impacted the ground.
